OBITUARY REFERENCE 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, I refer with profound sorrow to the passing 
away of Shri Narayanrao Krishnarao Shejwalkar, a former Member of this House on the 
23rd August, 2000 at the age of seventy-seven. 
Born at Gwalior in August, 1923, Shri Shejwalkar had his education at Gwalior 
and Agra. An Advocate by profession, Shri Shejwalkar was a member of the Civil 
Liberties Union and the M.B. Education Society, Gwalior. He was a member of the 
Municipal Corporation of Gwalior for eight years and was its Mayor in 1960, 1969 and 
1970. Shri Shejwalkar was also associated  with various social welfare and cultural 
organisations. 
Shri Shejwalkar represented the State of Madhya Pradesh in Rajya Sabha from 
April 1968 to April 1974. Shri Shejwalkar was also a Member of the Sixth and the 
Seventh Lok Sabhas. 
In the passing away of Shri Shejwalkar, the country has lost a noted social 
worker. 
We deeply mourn the passing away of Shri Shejwalkar. 
I request Members to rise in their places and observe silence as a mark of respect 
to the memory of the departed. 
(Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute.) 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Secretary-General will convey to the members of the 
bereaved family our deep sense of sorrow and sympathy.

Infrastructure of Dr. Bhimrao Babasaheb Ambedkar University 
*441. SHRI R.P. GOENKA: Will the Minister of HUM AN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Dr. Bhimrao Babasaheb Ambedkar University, Lucknow, 
established in 1989 and declared a Central University in 1996, has only 175 students on 
rolls and does not have even approach roads, entry gates etc.; 
(b) if so, the reasons for the apparent neglect and languishing of the Central 
University; and 
(c) the steps being taken to make the University functional for better utilisation 
of the infrastructure and the facilities created? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (DR. MURLI 
MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) to (c) According to the information furnished by the Babasaheb 
Bhimrao Ambedkar University (BBAU), Lucknow, its academic programmes were 
launched only in 1997 and the University has 159 students on its rolls during 1999-
2000. A motorable approach road to the University and the entry gates exist. The 
Central Government has provided Rs. 20.98 crores to this University since its inception 
for maintenance and development.

     Protection of water resources from industrial pollution 
†443. SHRI VUAY SINGH YADAV: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS be pleased to state: 
 whether Government propose to protect the water resources from industrial 
pollution; 
 if so, the details thereof; 
 whether Government have made an assessment of the quantum of water 
being rendered unfit to use every year due to industrial pollution; and 
 if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) and (b) The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 was 
enacted with the objective of protecting water resources from pollution. Under this Act, 
a State Pollution Control Board (SPCB) in every State and Pollution Control Committee 
(PCC) in every Union Territory and the Central Pollution Control Board for the entire 
country have been set up. Industrial units discharging effluents are required to take 
consent from the SPCB/PCC, and thereafter the consent has to be renewed 
periodically. 
(c) and (d) The CPCB have estimated the waste water generated from different 
categories of industries to be 83,140 million litres per day (mid), including 73,975 mid 
from thermal power plants. The industrial effluent, if treated appropriately, can be 
used fully or partially for specific purposes.

SHRI RAJIV RANJAN SINGH: 
Will the Minister of SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
 whether it is a fact that an experiment production of transgenic cotton was

 whether agro-scientists had conducted any study about the post-experiment

THE MINISTER OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY (DR. MURLI 
MANOHAR JOSHI): 
(a) to (d) Contained limited field experiments on transgenic cotton were carried 
out in various regions of the country. These experiments were not for production of 
transgenic cotton but were for evaluation of transgenic characters in cotton plants i. e. the 
effect of an introduced transgene that codes for a protein (Bt protein), produced by 
Bacillus thuringiensis, a bacterium commonly  
†Original  notice of the question  was  received  in  Hindi. 
28 

[25 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
occurring in nature. During 1998-2000, evaluation of agronomic performance and on-
farm trials for transgenic cotton to ascertain the yield, morphological characteristics, 
persistence, germination rate and pest load were carried out by the scientists of M/s 
Maharashtra Hybrid Seeds Co. Ltd. (MAHYCO), Mumbai in private lands and State 
Agricultural Universities in the State of Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Gujarat, 
Madhya Pradesh, Haryana, Punjab, Rajasthan and Tamil Nadu. The institutes were 
Acharya NG Ranga Agricultural University Rajendra Nagar, at its Regional Research 
Station, Lamb, Guntur, as well as at Warangal in Andhra Pradesh, Punjab Rao Krishi 
Vidyapeeth at Akola; and Marathwada Agricultural University, Parbhani in Maharashtra. 
The effect of Bt cottonseeds on goats as m odel was studied at the Indian Toxicological 
Research Centre (ITRC), Lucknow and Bt protein was not found to be toxic. The agro-
scientists of MAHYCO has conducted detailed post-harvest observations on the impact 
of Bt cotton cultivators at Ja lna in Maharashtra; Dharwad in Karnataka; Hyderabad in 
Andhra Pradesh and Coimbatore in Tamil Nadu. A team of over 20 scientists of R & D 
laboratory of MAHYCO led by Dr. Usha Zehr, Dr. S.K. Mukherjee and others 
conducted these experiments. It was concluded from these studies that there was 
significant increase in the yield from transgenic plants. There was also noticeable 
reduction in the spraying of chemical pesticides for bollworms, a major pest of cotton. 
The residues of Bt protein in soil were either non-existent or were extremely low and did 
not have any effect on the microbial popu lations of the soil samples. The Genetic 
Engineering Approval Committee has approved on 30lh June 2000, large scale field 
trials with scientific monitoring in some States. Work has started in the States of 
Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra.

*450. SHRI K. KALAVENKATA RAO: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
 whether the Draft National Population Policy is bereft of health 
infrastructure, in terms of inadequate co ntraceptive services, specialists and trained 
manpower and funding; and 
 if so, the action proposed to allocate more funds to run more health sub-
centres to achieve success of the family planning programme? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C.P. 
THAKUR): (a) and (b) The National Population Policy 2000 has specified that meeting 
unmet needs for contraception, health care infrastructure and health personnel and 
provision of integrated service delivery are the immediate objectives. Some of the 
operational strategies to achieve these objectives have been identified as follows :— 
(i)   Strengthening of the community health centres, primary health centres 
and sub-centres. 
(ii)   Strengthening of skills of health personnel and health providers. 
(iii) Maintenance at district and sub-di strict levels, block- wise database of 
private medical practitioners whose cr edentials may be certified by the 
Indian Medical Association. The possibility of accrediting these private 
practitioners for a year at a time, and assigning to each a satellite 
population, not exceeding 5000 population, for when they provide 
reproductive and child health services will be explored. 
(iv) Reviving the earlier system of the licensed medical practitioners who, after 
appropriate certificate from the Indian Medical Association, may 
participate in the provisional of clinical services. 
(v)   Involving the non-medical fraternity in counselling and advocacy so as to 
demystify the national family welfare efforts. 
35

stabilisation, a National Po pulation Stabilisation Fund with a seed money of Rs. 100

funds for supplies and equipment essential for meeting the unmet need for

*451. SHRI VIKRAM VERMA:

*456. SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
47 

RAJYA SABHA [25 August, 2000] 
 whether the Supreme Court has asked the Centre to submit report on death of 
twelve tigers in the Nandankanan Zoo in Orissa, recently; and 
 if so, the details of the probe report submitted and the action taken based on 
that report? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) and (b) Hon'ble Supreme Court directed the Ministry of Environment 
and Forests to place on record the report of the Committee which was appointed by the 
Ministry of Environment and Forests for inquiring into the death of tigers in 
Nandankanan Zoo and information as to the action taken thereupon. The Ministry of 
Environment and Forests has submitted a factual report to Hon'ble Supreme Court in 
this regard. The main recommendations of the report submitted by the Committee are as 
follows:— 
(i) Screening of tigers, lions and other animals should be conducted on a 
regular basis and appropriate treatment be provided on the basis of the 
screening results. 
(ii) Restraining facilities and isolation wards should be upgraded for 
effective treatment of the animals. 
(iii) Immediate repair of the safari and boundary wall to safeguard against 
ingress of livestock. 
(iv) All carnivores should be provided feed in individual feeding cells to 
ensure supply of food in hygien ic conditions and facilitating the 
physical handling of animals. 
(v)   Proper checking of the meat fed to the animals. 
(vi)   Improved cleanliness and better drainage. 
(vii) Officer of the level of at least Deputy Conservator of Forests should be 
stationed at part with adequate administrative and financial powers. 
(viii) Coordination between the Zoo Hospital and Orissa Veterinary College 
in matters of treatment of Zoo animals. 
On the basis of the above observations an d detailed consultations held with the 
State Government the following course of action has been agreed upon: 
48 

[25 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
 State Government would take necessary disciplinary action against the 
officials who were found lax in discharge of their duties. 
 Immediate action for reducing the overcrowding and providing each 
tiger/lion an individual feeding cells. 
 Periodic determination of parasitic loads in all the animals would be carried 
out and prophylactics would be provided wherever necessary. 
 The boundary wall of zoo and broken fencing of the Safari would be restored 
within three months. 
 Restraint facilities and the isolation wards attached to the zoo hospital would 
be upgraded immediately. 
(0 System for regular checking of the quality of meat and drinking water for the 
animals would be in place. 
(g) the hygiene and sanitation of the zoo shall be improved. 
(h) A panel of veterinarians and experts would be constituted for monitoring 
the implementation of the above recommendations. 
(i) State Government would permit direct flow of funds from the Central Zoo 
Authority to the zoo to avoid delay in execution of work of essential nature.

Interim Report on the death of tigers 
*459. SHRI KULDIP NAYYAR: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS be pleased to state: 
 whether interim report on the death of tigers in the Nandankanan Zoo has 
been received; 
 if so, what are the contents thereof; and 
 what steps are being taken to reduce the number of tigers and other animals 
in over populated zoos? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) and (b) Ministry of Environment and Forests have received the report of 
the Committee which was constituted to ascertain the causes of deaths of tigers and to 
suggest ways to avoid recurrence of the same in Nandankanan Zoo, Orissa. The report 
has confirmed that the main cause of the death of tigers was 'Trypanosomiasis'. It has 
confirmed that the choice of the drug 'Berenil' used by the Zoo Administration was 
appropriate. It has also been observed that a large number of tigers in the zoo, lack of 
proper hygiene, and the onset of monsoon caused the increase in the incidence of 
vectors. The main recommendations of the report submitted by the Committee are as as 
follows:— 
(i) Screening of tigers, lions and other animals should be conducted on a 
regular basis and appropriate treatment be provided on the basis of the 
screening results. 
(ii) Restraining facilities and isolat ion wards should be upgraded for 
effective treatment of the animals. 
(iii) Immediate repair of the safari an d boundary wall to safeguard against 
ingress of livestock. 
(iv) All carnivores should be provided feed in individual feeding cells to 
ensure supply of food in hygienic conditions and facilitating the 
physical handling of animals. 
(v)   Proper checking of the meat fed to the animals. 
(vi)   Improved cleanliness and better drainage. 
(vii) Officer of the level of at least Deputy Conservator of Forests should be 
stationed at part with adequate administrative and financial powers.

in matters of treatment of zoo animals.

3418. SHRI CM. IBRAHIM: Will the Minister of CHEMICALS AND 
FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
 whether, in order to offset the loss to  the domestic industry, consequent on

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS AND 
FERTILIZERS (SHRI RAMESH BAIS): (a) to (c) Urea is the only fertilizer which is 
under price, movement and distribution control and whose imports are made on 
Government account. The Quantitative Restrictions (QRs) on urea have to be lifted w.e.f. 
1.4.2001. The freeing of QRs, including those on urea, is a commitment India has 
entered into in an Agreement with USA in December, 1999 following the ruling of the 
Dispute Settlement Body of the WTO that 
58 

[25 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
India's QRs were not justified on balance of payments grounds. The Government has set 
up a Task Force to study the impact of removal of QRs on urea and suggest measures 
including that of bound rate which will be made applicable to protect the indigenous 
industry. The recommendations of the Tasks Force will form the basis for imposition 
of applied rate of tariff on urea imports. 
All other major fertilizers are decontrolled and their imports are being freely 
made on private trade account. Currently, tariff on Di-Ammonium Phosphate (DAP) 
and Sulphate of Potash (SOP) is 5% while it is 5.5% in respect of other fertilizers.

Essential Commodities Act In respect of decontrolled fertilizers, the Government has been fixing 
MRP under the Concession Scheme which is administered by the Department of Agriculture 
and Cooperation. So long as this arrangement continues, levying of tariff may have no 
impact on the market prices.

Ganga Action Plan 
3429. SHRI PARMESHWAR KUMAR AGARWALLA: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
 what is the present stage of Ganga Action Plan; 
 to what extent Ganga has been purified; and 
 at the present rate, how long it will take to complete the Ganga Action Plan? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS (SHRI BABU LAL MARANDI): (a) The Ganga Action Plan has been taken up in 
two phases. Under the first phase started in June 1985 at a cost of Rs. 462.04 crore, an 
amount of Rs. 451.70 crore has been utilised by the Go vernment of India. In addition 
an amount of Rs. 477.25 crore has been utilised so far out of allocated funds of Rs. 
1276.26 crore on the second phase of the Ganga Action Plan approved in stages 
between 1993 to 1996. 
(b) The target fixed for the implementation of the Ganga Action Plan Phase I 
was to bring the water quality of the river Ganga to the "bathing class" standards which 
is as under:  
Bio-chemical Oxygen Demand (BOD) 3 mg/1 (maximum) 
Dissolved Oxygen (DO) 5 mg/1 (minimum) 
Total Coliform (MPN) 10,000 per 100 ml 
Fecal Coliform (MPN) 2,500 per 100 ml 
The present level of Bio-chemical oxygen demand, an indicator of pollution is 
lower than the level in 1986, The range of Bio-chemcial oxygen demand level which 
was 1.7 to 15.5 in 1986 has come down to 1.0 to 6.5 in 1999. The range of dissolved 
oxygen level which was 5.6 to 8.4 in 1986 has risen to 7.1 to 9.0 in 1999. However, 
there has been only an incidental reduction in the level of microbial pollution of the 
treated sewage reaching the river. A total of 835 million litre per day of sewage has 
been intercepted for treatment under the Ganga Action Plan Phase I upto 2000. With 
the completion of the Ganga Action Plan Phase I, only about 35% of the pollution 
generated from towns located along the Ganga has been tackled. The remaining 
pollution is to be tackled under the Ganga Action Plan Phase II which is already under 
70 

[25 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
execution. Under this phase, interception and treatment of 1861 million litre per day of 
sewage is proposed. 
(c) While the Ganga Action Plan Phase I has been declared closed since 
31.3.2000, the Ganga Action Plan Phase II is likely to be completed by 2005.

projected by the seven CGHS dispensaries.

being any demand from the user dispensaries Besides, the Additional Director CGHS 
Pune had to divert medicines valued at Rs. 14.51 lakh to CGHS dispensaries at other 
locations and a Government Hospital to avoid their time expiry.

3461. SHRI K. KALAVEKATA RAO: 
DR. DASARI NARAYANA RAO: 
SHRI SOLIPETA RAMACHANDRA REDDY: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
98 

[25 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
 wheather Madhya Pradesh Government is giving a lead in population control 
by denying all the benefits and facilities under Government schemes to parents giving 
birth to third child after January 26, 2000; and 
 if so, the seriousness of Union Government to announce such a new 
population stabilization policy and extend it to cover all Union Government Offices 
and elected offices like Panchayats, cooperative institutions, etc.? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE [DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMA]: (a) Population Policy adopted 
by Government of Madhya Pradesh envisages that Persons having more than two 
children after January 26, 2001 would not be eligible for contesting election for 
Panchayats, local bodies, mandis or cooperatives in the State. In case, they get elected 
and in the mean time they have the third child, they would be disqualified for that post. 
(b) The National Population Policy 2000 adopted in February 2000 affirms 
commitment of Government towards voluntary and informed choice and consent of 
citizens while availing of reproductive hea lth case service, and continuation of the 
target free approach in administering family planning services. 
A Central Bill, titled the Constitution Seventy-Ninth (Amendment) Bill, 1992 
was introduced in the Rajya Sabha on December, 1992. The Bill seeks to amend the 
Directive Principles of State Policy to provide that the State shall endeavour to 
promote population control and the small family norm and to include in the 
Fundamental Duties, a duty to promote and adopt the small family norm. It is also 
proposed that a person shall be disqualified for being chosen as, and for being, a 
member of either House of Parliament or eith er House of Legislature of a State, if he 
has more than two children. 
While recommending the Bill for passage, the Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Human Resource Development also recommended that the 
Government may convene a meeting of leaders of various political parties in 
Parliament to ensure the smooth passage of the Bill. 
Accordingly, meet ings of the political parties were held under the 
chairpersonship of MOS(H and FW) on 14th August, 1997 and in December 1999, to 
evolve a consensus for its smooth passage in the Parliament. However, so far, there is no 
consensus among the major political parties, on the subject.

†3493. SHRI SURESH PACHOURI: 
SHRI BALKAVI BAIRAGI: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
 whether the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare had issued a notification 
in the Gazette of India on 11 th October, 1999 for use of animal raw material in the tea-
flavour; 
 if so, the names of persons responsible for the same; and 
 what amendments were made in that notification and when? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE [DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMA]: (a) to (c) Prior to the 
notification of an amendment to the Preven tion of Food Adulteration (PFA) Rules on 
11.10.99, under entries A. Hand A. 14.01 of Appendix B of the PFA 
†Original  notice of the question  was  received  in  Hindi. 
127 

RAJYA SABHA [25 August, 2000] 
Rules, 1955, only certain flavours were permissible for producing flavoured tea. There 
was a demand from the tea industry that, with the increasing variety of niche products in 
the market, there was a need to give more flexibility as to the types of flavours which 
may be added to tea. As a result, a notification was issued on 11.10.99, after obtaining 
the recommendations of the Central Committee for Food Standards, deleting the 
limited list of specific flavours permissible for tea. This, in result, made tea subject to 
the general provision for flavours under Rule 63 of the PFA Rules, which applies to all 
items for which there are no specific provis ions. Under Rule 63 of the PFA Rules, the 
products may be flavoured with substances of vegetable or animal origin. 
Since 9.8.94, the PFA Rules, 1955 have included a provision under Rule 44(G) 
under which, inter-alia flavoured tea can only be sold by those manufacturers who are 
registered with the Tea Board. This provision has never been lifted since its inclusion in 
the Rules. Therefore, even after the amendment to entry A. 14 to Appendix B in respect of 
permissible flavours for tea, permission from the Tea Board for adding flavours, was 
necessary before introducing any new flavour for tea. It has been confirmed by the 
competent authorities in the Tea Board that no tea manufacturing company has asked 
for permission for adding flavours containing ingredients of animal origin and no such 
permission has been given by them. 
However, to forestall any misinterpretation of the existing provisions, under 
notification dated 2.08.2000, items A.14 and A.14.01 of Appendix B of the PFA Rules 
have been amended to make it explicit that the flavouring substances permissible in tea 
will be exclusively of materials of vegetable origin. 
The amendments to the PFA Rules including the one made on 11-10-1999 are 
made following the statutory process prescribed for this purpose, which includes 
consultation with the Central Committee for Food Standards (CCFS) comprising 
representatives from State Governments, experts, represen-tatives from other related 
departments of Government etc. vetting by the Ministry of Law and prepublication of 
the draft notification when comments/ objections from the public are invited and 
considered before the final notification is published.

country, including Assam to control Malaria and other vector-borne diseases. Apart 
from primary health care services delivered by State/UT Goyemment(s), the tea garden 
authorities also have the health infrastructure for rendering health care delivery to the 
tea garden population. These health care services are also supplemented by the State 
Health authorities by deputing medical teams at the time of outbreaks and also by 
providing requisite services as per need.

adjoining areas of Assam have been carried out and the State Government and tea 
garden authorities are assisted in training of doctors and para-medical staff for 
management of diarrheal diseases. Besides, community directed health education camps 
are held in tea gardens for spreading awareness on communicable diseases.

Distortions in Text books 
3508. SHRI KRISHNA KUMAR BIRLA: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
 whether it is a fact that text books prescribed for educational Institutes in 
certain States in the country continue to contain distortions making the impressionable 
minds of students biased against the minority communities; 
 if so, how continuance of such biased school text books can create healthy 
atmosphere and cordial relationship among various communities and sections of 
society in a secular and democratic country; and 
 what measures are contemplated by Government in this direction? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (DR. MURLI 
MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) to (c) The Nation al Policy on Education envisages a 
National System of Education based on a National Curricular Framework containing a 
common core cutting across different subject areas. Based on the framework 
guidelines and the revised textbooks of the NCERT, the State Governments are 
expected to adopt or adapt, the same for revision of school curricula, syllabi and 
textbooks in their respective school systems in a phased manner. An overwhelming 
majority of the schools in the country are under the control of State Governments and 
they enjoy full autonomy in all school education matters, including prescription of 
syllabi and textbooks within their respective jurisdiction. Whenever any objectionable 
references are brought to the notice of the Union Government, the matter is referred to 
the States for necessary action. The Central Government or its organisations do not have 
any direct role in this matter.

3521. SHRI N.K. PREMA CHANDRAN: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
 what are the major recommendations of Rastogi Commission Report; 
 whether UGC has exempted Ph. D. (Degree) holders from National 
Eligibility Test on the basis of the recommendation of Rastogi Commission; and 
154 

[25 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (DR. MURLI 
MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) The major recommendations made by Rastogi Committee 
regarding revision of pay scales and service conditions of teachers in universities and 
colleges are as follows: 
 Good academic record, 55% at the Master's level and qualifying the NET 
or an accredited test should be the minimum qualification for the 
appointment of lecturers. 
 The probation should normally be for a period of 24 months, extendable 
upto a further period of 12 months in case of unsatisfactory performance. 
 Posts of professors be provided in the postgraduate colleges. 
 There is need for introducing the concept of pre-induction training 
programmes for the teachers through academic staff colleges. 
 For placement in the senior scale, a lecturer may offer himself/ herself 
for review after 4 years in holding a Ph. D. degree and 6 years if holding 
an M. Phil degree and 7 years if not holding M.Phil/ Ph.D. 
 A Lecturer (Scale) can offer himself/herself for review after 6 years of 
experience as Senior Lecturer, for placement in the Selection Grade. 
 The Merit Promotion Scheme, having dual emoluments or, for the matter, 
any such scheme be dispensed with. 
The Universities/Colleges must observe 180 actual teaching days. 
UGC guidelines regarding minimum number of actual teaching days, 
programme of examination reform and workload for teachers in the 
Universities and Colleges issued in 1989 prescribed that the workload of a 
teacher in full employment should not be less than 40 hours a week for 30 
working weeks in an academic year, which should be ensured. 
The practice of appointing part-time teachers should be sparingly used 
and the remuneration given for such work must be based on realistic 
norms.

As per sixth All India Educational Survey (1993) 83.73% primary schools and 
89.30% upper primary schools had pucca and partly pucca buildings.

Under the Scheme of Operation Blackboard (OB), 1.82 lakhs classrooms have 
been constructed and financial assistan ce for Teaching Learning Equipment (TLE) 
including black boards has been provided to 5,22,902 primary schools and to 127,257

District Primary Education Programme (DPEP) is currently in operation in 219 
districts in 15 States. It provides for improvement of physical infrastructure facilities 
and manpower resources in primary school. Under this programme 8,000 formal 
school have been added and another 15,000 are in pipeline. 38,000 alternative 
schooling centres of various kinds have been set up and about 75,000 more are 
planned. A new scheme Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan has now been proposed to achieve 
holistic convergence of all schemes/ programmes of elementary education to provide 
education to all children in the age group of 6.14 years by the year 2010.

Appeal Rules and punishment imposed upon them. To prevent train accidents,

RAJYA SABHA [25 August, 2000] 
following steps are being taken for improvement of staff functioning and equipment 
reliability. 
(i) The work of track circuiting has been accelerated on the trunk routes 
and other important main lines. Fouling Mark to Fouling Mark track 
circuiting work has been completed on A, B, C, D Spl. and D routes. 
(ii) Modification of the signalling circuitry is being carried out to minimise 
chances of human error in causing accidents. 
(iii) Auxiliary Warning System for givi ng advance warning about 'Signal at 
danger' to the driver of the running train has been commissioned on 
Mumbai suburban sections. 
(iv) There has been progressive increase in use of Tie Tamping and ballast 
cleaning machines for track maintenance. 
(v) For monitoring track geometry and running characteristics of the track, 
sophisticated track recording cars, oscillograph cars and portable 
accelerometers are being progressively used. 
(vi) Maintenance facilities for coaches and wagons have been modernised 
and upgraded at many depots. 
(vii) To prevent cases of cold breakage of axles, routine over hauling depots 
have been equipped with ultrasonic testing equipment for detection of 
flaws in the axles. 
(viii) Whistle boards/speed breakers and road signs have been provided at 
unmanned level crossings and visibility for drivers has been improved. 
(ix) Audio-visual publicity campaigns to educate road users on how to make 
a safe crossing are conducted. 
(x) Steps have been taken to prevent inflammable and explosive materials 
from being carried in passenger trains. 
(xi) Training facilities for drivers, guards and staff connected with train 
operation have been modernised including use of Simulators for 
training of drivers. 
(xii)   Refresher courses are regularly organised at specified intervals.

RAJ MOHINDER SINGH:

 whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news item published

 if so, whether it is a fact that many scientific institutions of certain developed 
and developing countries have expressed concern over transgenic food crops; and 
 if so, Government's reaction in this regard?  
†Original  notice of the question  was  received  in  Hindi. 
194 

[25 August, 2000] RA JYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY IN THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY (SHRI BACHI 
SINGH RAWAT): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) The Science Academies around the world including U.K., U.S., 
Brazil, China, Mexico, India and Third World Academy of Sciences have discussed 
various aspects of Transgenic Plants and World Agriculture. Their views are that for 
improving food production and for reducing environmental impacts, a proper 
responsible utilization of scientific discoveries and new technologies are necessary. 
Food can be produced through the use of Genetically Modified technology that are more 
nutritious, stable in storage and in principle, health promoting and bringing benefits to 
consumers in both developing and industrialised nations. Co-operative efforts between 
private and public sectors are needful to develop new transgenic crops that benefit 
consumers, especially in the developing world. Public health regulatory systems need to 
be in place for monitoring the impacts of transgenics. The Academies have welcomed 
Genetically Modified crop technology and have recommended that the technology be 
adopted both by the developed and the developing countries with adequate biosafety 
regulations. The report of the Scientific Academies is a balanced publication. Biosafety 
Guidelines in India are exhaustive and adequate to assess the risks, if any, from the use 
of GM crops to the environment including human and animal health. GM crops can be 
introduced into commercial agriculture only after assessing their safety and agronomic 
advantages.

3561. SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: Will the Minister of SCIENCE

 the details of operational services provided by the Ministry in the field of

 the steps taken or proposed to be taken to report and forecast weather

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY IN THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY (SHRI BACHI 
SINGH RAWAT): (a) India Meteorological Department (IMD) is the principal 
Government Agency in all matters related to meteorology and allied fields in the 
country. IMD's operational responsibilities are: 
 To operate and maintain a network of meteorological observatories. 
 To operate and maintain a telecommunication network for collection and 
dissemination of meteorological data within and outside the country. 
 To issue weather forecasts for the public and users in specific sectors such as 
agriculture, aviation, shipping, fisheries, off-shore oil exploration, etc. 
 To issue warnings against natural disasters like Tropical Cyclones and to 
assist other Disaster Management Agencies including Flood Forecasting. 
 To archive climate data and supply past data to users. 
196 

[25 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
Survey of India (SOI) is the principal mapping agency of this country and it is 
responsible for ensuring that the country's domain is explored and mapped suitably to 
provide base maps for expeditious and integrated development. SOI provides the 
following services:— 
 To produce all purpose topographical maps required for defence, general 
administration, internal security, developmental needs, irrigation and 
different types of engineering projects. 
 To produce other maps viz. District  Planning Map Series, Tourist Maps, 
Trekking Maps and small scale geographical maps. 
 To carry out project surveys on larger scales according to the 
specifications of the development projects. 
 To provide an accurate positional framework for all significant points on 
earth's surface, especially in and around India. 
 To make use of low altitude remotely sense imageries for topographical 
interpretation and mapping. 
In addition SOI provides the following services in the field of meteorology:— 
 Tidal data on East and West coast, Andaman and Nicobar Islands and 
Lakshadweep Islands is being collected through a network of tidal 
observatories for prediction of tides about one year in advance for the 
purpose of navigational activities and study of variation in mean sea-level. 
 The mapping on 1:25,000 scale with half metre contour interval under 
Coastal Mapping Programme on the East Coast (Nellore to Bangladesh 
Border) in order to study the effect of submergence due to rise in sea-
level and other natural phenomena i.e. Storm surges, cyclones etc. has 
been completed. 
The National Atlas and Thematic Mapping Organization (NATMO) provides 
the following services:— 
 To compile the National Atlas of India in English and Hindi. 
 To prepare National Atlas Maps in regional languages. 
 To prepare Thematic Maps based on research studies on 
197 

RAJYA SABHA [25 August, 2000] 
environmental and associated aspects and their impact on social and 
economic development. 
NATMO does not provide any operational services in the field of Meteorology. 
However, in the District Planning Maps, there is an inset depicting the climatic conditions 
of the concerned district. 
In addition to the above, the National Centre for Medium Range Weather 
Forecasting (NCMRWF), New Delhi is providing medium range weather forecast (3—4 
days in advance) based Agrometeorological Advisory Service (AAS) to the farmers 
through 81 AAS units located all over the country. 
 A proven and reliable system for dissemination of district-wise weather 
information and cyclone warnings is already in operation in coastal districts. Under the 
INSAT based Cyclone Warning Dissemination System (CWDS), a total of 250 receiver 
sets have been installed in various coastal districts. The information is disseminated to 
State and Central Government Agencies and to the public through All India Radio and 
Doordarshan, in addition to use of fax/ telephone, high priority telegrams, teleprinter and 
telex messages, police wireless and Newspapers. Farmers' Weather Bulletins are issued 
daily and broadcast from AIR Stations. These bulletins contain district wise weather 
forecasts for next 48 hours with outlook for subsequent two days. IMD issues bi-
weekly agro-meteorological advisories from 17 centres located in state capitals. These 
include district-wise information and are broadcast from AIR stations and also telecast 
from Doordarshan Kendras. In addition there are special programmes arranged on AIR 
and Doordarshan for promoting use of weather information in various agricultural 
practices. 
 State-of-art technology such as Satellite, Radar and Computer Systems is being 
used for weather observation, data exchange, data processing and weather forecasting. 
The INSAT system has been fully exploited for meteorological analysis and weather 
forecasting. A system of 10 S-band conventional radars covers both east and west coasts 
of the country and provides powerful surveillance for detection of tropical cyclones. 
Regional Telecommunication Hub (RTH) under World Meteorological Organization 
has been upgraded to enhance the speed and quantum of data reception and exchange. 
IMD has launched its own internet website (http;//www.imd.emet.in) for dissemination of 
weather information, weather charts and satellite images. Regional Websites have also

prepared using a high speed Super

STATEMENT-I 
Salient Features of the Scheme 
1.      Applicability of the Scheme: 
Scheme is for implementation by Commercial banks, Regional Rural Banks 
and Cooperative banks (District Central Cooperative Banks/Primary 
212 

[25 August, 2000] R AJYA SABHA 
Agriculture Cooperative Societies). Implementing banks have the discretion to adopt 
the same to suit location specific requirements. 
2. Objective: 
Kisan Credit Card Scheme aims at adequate and timely support from the banking 
system to the farmers for their cultivation needs including purchase of all inputs in a 
flexible and cost effective manner. 
3. Eligibility: 
The scheme would primarily cater to the short term credit requirements of the 
farmers. Under the scheme, banks may provide the Kisan Credit Cards to farmers who 
are eligible for sanction of production credit. There is no upper and lower limit. 
4. Issue of cards: 
The beneficiaries under the scheme will be issued credit card and pass books or 
credit card-cum- passbooks, incorporating the name, address, particulars of land 
holding, borrowing limit, validity period, etc. which will serve both as an identity card 
as well as facilitate recording of transactions on an on-going basis. 
5. Fixation of credit limit: 
The credit extended under the Kisan Credit Card Scheme is in the nature of 
revolving cash credit and provide for any number of drawals and repayments within the 
limit. While fixing the limits, the entire credit requirements of the farmers for the full 
year are to be taken into account. The credit limit under the card is to be fixed on the 
basis of the operational land holding, cropping pattern and scale of finance as 
recommended by District Level/State Level Committee. 
6. Validity/renewal: 
The validity of the credit card normally should be for a period of 3 years subject 
to an annual review. 
7. Rate of interest: 
Rates of interest are to be charged as applicable to crop loans.

Security/margin norms should be in conformity with the instructions issued by

Launching of PMGY 
*425. CHAUDHARY CHUNNI LAL: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased 
to state: 
 whether a new "Pradhan Mantri Gramodaya Yojana" has been launched 
recently; 
 if so, the salient features thereof; 
 the criteria fixed for disbursement of funds to the States under the Scheme; 
and 
 the allocation made during the current year State-wise and the results achieved 
during the last three months? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING AND 
MINISTER OF STATE OF MINISTRY  OF STATISTICS AND PROGRAMME 
IMPLEMENTATION AND MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF 
ADMINISTRATIVE REFORMS AND PUBLIC GRIEVANCES OF THE MINISTRY 
OF PERSONNEL, PUBLIC GRIEVANCES AND PENSIONS AND MINISTER OF 
STATE OF THE DEPARTMENT OF DISINVESTMENT (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) In order to achieve the objective of sustainable human development at the 
village level, Pradhan Mantri  Gramodaya Yojana (PMGY) has been launched in the 
Annual Plan 2000-01 in all the States and UTs. 
PMGY envisages allocation of Additional Central Assistance (ACA) to the 
States and UTs for selected basic minimum services. The allocation for PMGY in the 
current year is Rs. 5000 crore. PMGY has two components, namely, rural roads and other 
programmes of PMGY. While the rural roads programme has been allocated Rs. 2500 
crore, the other Programmes of PMGY have also been allocated an equal amount of Rs. 
2500 crore. The rural roads component 
216 

[25 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
of the PMGY is being coordinated by the Department of Rural Development. For the 
other sectoral programmes of PMGY, the concerned Central Administrative 
Departments of Elementary Education and Literacy, Family Welfare, Drinking Water, 
Rural Development and Women and Child Development are responsible for 
coordination and supervision. These Departments have issued guidelines for 
implementation of their sectoral programmes by the State Governments under PMGY. 
As per the guidelines, a minimum of 15 per cent of the ACA allocation of a State must 
be allocated to each of the five sectors under other programmes of PMGY. While 75 per 
cent of the ACA allocation of a State will be spent on the five sectors, the allocation of 
the residual 25 per cent of the ACA will be decided by the States and UTs themselves 
as per their own priorities. 
While the other programmes of PMGY would also be monitored by these Central 
Departments, the overall monitoring of the PMGY would be undertaken by the Planning 
Commission. 
(c) In so far as Special Category States are concerned, approximately 30 
per cent of the total allocation under the other programmes of PMGY has been 
kept aside and distributed among these States on the basis of their proportionate 
share as worked out for the devolution of the normal Central Assistance. 
The relative gaps in the basic services infrastructure/indicator among the States 
have been taken as the criteria for disbursement of the remaining 70 per cent of funds 
among the Non-Special Category States under PMGY. The four sectors which have 
been taken to calculate a State-specific composite weighted average index are Drinking 
Water, Primary Health, Primary Education and Shelter. Each of the four sectors has 
been given equal weightage. As per this criteria, the States which rank low stand to gain 
by a relatively higher allocation of ACA for PMGY. 
The allocation for the rural roads component of PMGY is yet to be finalised by the 
Department of Rural Development. 
(d) The State-wise allocation of ACA made for the current year for the 
other programmes of PMGY is given in the Statement. The first six monthly 
instalments of ACA for all the five sectors to all States and UTs have been 
released during June-July, 2000.

Signing of NPT 
*434. SHRI KARA. SUBBIAN: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
 whether it is a fact that only four nations—Cuba, Israel, Pakistan and India 
have not signed Nuclear Non-proliferation Treaty (NPT); 
 if so, whether it will have any negative effect on India; 
 what is the outcome of the month-long NPT Review Conference; and 
 whether UN Security Council or the NPT Conference exerted pressure on 
India to become a member of the NPT? 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JASWANT SINGH) (a) Yes, 
Sir. 
 This is India's considered and consistent position. 
 The 6th Review Conference of the NPT held in New York from 24th 
April—20th May concluded with the adoption a final document. Although the document 
has a reference to an "unequivocal undertaking" on nuclear disarmament and some 
practical steps to further nuclear disarmament under Article VI of the treaty, there is, 
however, no substantive change in the position of the NPT nuclear weapon States on 
nuclear disarmament. 
 The final document of the NPT Review Conference recalls UN Security Council 
resolution 1172 and calls on India to undertake the measures set out in that resolution 
and to accede to the NPT as a non-nuclear weapon State. India has rejected UN 
Security Council resolution 1172 and maintains that the NPT Community needs to come 
to terms with the realty that India is a nuclear weapon State.

Restructuring National Seeds Corporation of India 
3256. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether there is a proposal to restructure the National Seeds Corporation 
of India; 
 what is the present operational activity of the National Seeds Corporation; 
 whether it is a fact that various Committees have recommended a total 
restructuring of this Corporation; 
 what role does Government see for the NSC in view of the new 
Agricultural Policy charting a course over the next 20 years; and 
 the details of the present role and future role of the National Seeds 
Corporation? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI 
S.B.P.B.K. SATYANARAYANA RAO): (a) The Government of India have appointed 
M/s SBI Capital Market Ltd., Mumbai as Consultant to study reorganising and 
revitalizing of NSC. 
(b) The present operational activity of the National Seeds Corporation is 
as under:— 
 Organising production and distribution of foundation and certified seed of 
Cereals, Pulses, Fibre and Vegetable crops by supplementing the production 
by other agencies mainly through contract growers. 
 Production and supply of seeds to North Eastern Region and other States 
whose topography is not conducive to seed production. 
 Installation and operation of seed processing plants and seed storage 
structure. 
 Preserving a buffer stock of seeds of principal crops. 
 Training and education on seed. 
(c) M/s Tata Consultancy Services were appointed as Operating 
Consultant in 1990 for conducting management study of the Corporation. 
Based on the recommendations, structural changes like introduction of Voluntary 
Retirement Scheme to reduce surplus manpower and repayment of loans to Commercial Banks 
and Government of India has already been carried out. 
239 

RAJYA SABHA [25 August, 2000] 
 In order to fulfil the national endeavour of adequate and timely supply of 
quality seeds at reasonable prices to the farmers, the National Seeds Corporation will be 
restructured for efficient utilization of investment and manpower. The restructuring 
would be in terms of augmenting the infrast ructure of production and distribution of 
improved varieties of quality seeds and planting material. 
 The present role of the Corporation is: 
 
 To produce and distribute seeds of high quality to the farmers. 
 To bring about awareness among the farming community towards 
utilization of high quality seeds. 
 Fulfilling a social obligation of producing and distributing seed of such 
crops which are not commercially profitable. 
In future, the Corporation will aspire:— 
 To be a leader in the field of production, multiplication, distribution and 
related activities in the area of quality seeds through efficient and optimum 
use of resources. 
 To diversify the product mix in favour of high value-low volume seeds to 
further improve the profitability of the Corporation. 
 To enter technology partnerships with internal and external organizations to 
promote high quality genetic material in seed production. 
 To explore diversification to tissue culture, bio-technology etc. 
Fertility of Agricultural Land 
†3257. SHRI BACHANI LEKHRAJ: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be 
pleased to state: 
 whether it is a fact that the fertility of agricultural land is decreasing 
continuously; 
 if so, whether Government are contemplating to take measures for 
increasing the fertility of agricultural land in various parts of the country; and 
 if so, the outline thereof and if not, in which manner Government intend 
to solve this problem? 
†Original  notice of the question was received  in  Hindi. 
240 

[25 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI 
S.B.P.B.K. SATYANARAYANA RAO): (a) Yes, Sir. Intensive cropping with high inputs 
and high yielding varieties have resulted in decline in soil fertility, particularly in 
respect of micro and secondary nutrients elements due to their removal at a rate more 
than their replenishment. 
(b) and (c) Generally, the fertility of soils improves with improvement in moisture 
availability in the soil. The Department of Agriculture and Cooperation is advocating soil 
and water conservation and soil test based balanced and integrated nutrient 
management through conjunctive use of both inorganic and organic sources of plant 
nutrients to restore soil fertility. 
The Department of Agriculture and Co operation is implementing various land 
based programmes, namely (i) Soil Conservation in the catchments of River Valley 
Projects (RVP) and Flood Prone Rivers (FPR), (ii) Watershed Development Project in 
Shifting Cultivation Areas, (iii) National Watershed Development Project in Rainfed 
Areas and (iv) Reclamation of Alkali Soils, to minimise land degradation which 
ultimately results in enhan ced fertility in the agricultur al land of the country. In 
addition to the above, the State Governments implement their own Plan Schemes for 
improving fertility of such areas in their States.

Protection of Sugarcane Industries in Maharashtra 
3260. MISS MABEL REBELLO: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be 
pleased to state: 
 whether Government have any proposal to protect the sugarcane industry in 
Maharashtra; 
 if so, what action has been taken so far to implement the proposal; 
 the Government have any suggestion to export sugar out of India; and 
 what is the response from Western countries? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI 
S.B.P.B.K. SATYANARAYANA RAO): (a) and (b) Due to unprecedented large sugar 
production during the current 1999-2000 (October-September) sugar season in the country 
in general and Maharashtra in particular, the sugar industry is facing problem of liquidity 
both in terms of storage space and finances. With a view to easing out the problem, the 
Government have taken following measures: 
(i) The Central Government have reduced the levy obligation of domestic sugar 
factories from 40% to 30% with effect from 1.1.2000 with a view to 
improving the financial position of the sugar factories which would enable 
them to pay the cane price dues promptly. 
(ii) To restrict inflow of imported Sugar in the country, Government with effect 
from 9.2.2000, have increased the custom duty to 60% along with the 
existing countervailing duty of Rs. 850 per tonne. 
(iii) The Central Government is also pursuing a policy of encouraging stability 
and reasonable level of sugar prices in the domestic market through 
judicious releases of free sale sugar quotas to enable the sugar factories to 
clear the cane price dues of the farmers. 
(iv) Advance release of free sale sugar are being made to the needy sugar 
factories enabling them to pay the cane price dues, (v)  Due to non-lifting of levy 
sugar by FCI from certain States including Maharashtra, an equivalent quantity 
was released as advance freesale sugar for sale in the open market.

(c) and (d) Government have decided to allow export of 10 lakh tonnes of sugar 
and not charge levy on the export quantity for a period of six months with effect from 1 st

quantities for Bangladesh and Sri Lanka.

 whether Government are aware of newsitem captioned "Gujarat farmer's organic 
farming began 40 years ago" appeared in The Hindustan Times, on 16th June, 2000;

cent without using fertilizers and pesticides in his "Kalpavrukhsa" farm;

S.B.P.B.K. SATYANARAYANA RAO): (a) to (d) It has been reported in The 
Hindustan Times dated 16.6.2000 mat one Shri Bhaskar Hiraji Save has been 
practicing only organic farming for the last over 40 years. He is not using any 
fertilizers, insecticides, weedicides and does not resort to tilling of the land. He uses 
plant leaves and organic wastes as source of plant nutrients, encourages the growth of 
earth worms for tilling the soil and natural in sects and birds for killing the crop pests. 
As per the information from State Government, good levels of crop yields are obtained 
at this farm. However, the information about levels of profitability is not indicated. The 
State Government recommends the use of fertilizers as per the soil test based 
recommendations and also encourages the farmers for use of compost and biofertilisers.

Reduction of Economic cost of FCI 
†3308.   SHRI KAPIL SIBAL: 
SHRI RAJIV RANJAN SINGH: 
Will the Minister of CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
 whether the Government have sought suggestions during last three years to 
reduce the economic cost of Food Corporation of India; 
 if so, the names of institutions alongw ith the suggestions given by them to 
the Government; and 
 the action taken by the Government to implement those suggestions? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS 
AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHRIRAM CHAUHAN): (a) to (c) The 
Administrative Staff College of India, Hyderabad has been engaged to study the cost of 
acquisition and distribution of wheat and rice by the Food Corporation of India so as to 
arrive at ways and means to reduce its Economic Cost of wheat and rice. The final report 
of the College is expected by the end of September, 2000 only. 
However, in the meanwhile the Expenditure Reforms Commission which was set 
up by the Government of India in February, 2000 has re-viewed the methodology of 
allocation of distribution cost between stocks maintained by the Food Corporation of 
India for distribution through Public Distribution System and buffer stocks. The 
Commission has made three important changes in the methodology. 
(i) At present, only, the annual accretion to the buffer stocks is reckoned for 
allocation of distribution cost. However, considering that it would be necessary for 
Government to rotate the stocks held as buffer stocks over a two to three year period in 
the interest of maintaining quality, the Commission has recommended that transport cost 
and transit losses to the extent of one-third of the opening stocks of buffer be charged to 
the buffer carrying cost. 
(ii) The Commission has felt that carry over charges, namely, charges paid to 
the State agencies involved in the procurement of wheat beyond 30th June every year, 
should be part of the buffer carrying cost rather than economic cost of wheat for public 
distribution. 
†Original  notice  of the q ue stion   was  received  in  H indi. 
296 

[25 August, 2000] RA JYA SABHA 
(iii) The Commission has also recommended  that the economic cost should be 
estimated on the basis of pooling of opening stocks available with the Food 
Corporation of India in the beginning of the year and stocks procured during the current 
year, rather than being based on the minimum support price of the current year. 
On account of these changes in the methodology, which have been accepted by 
Government, the economic cost of wheat and rice for public distribution have been 
revised to Rs. 830 per quintal for wheat instead of Rs. 900 per quintal as before and to 
Rs. 1,130 per quintal for rice instead of Rs. 1,180 per quintal as originally estimated.

evidence of Indian extremist elements from Punjab and Kashmir, with the help of ISI,

the decisions taken in these meetings, both sides have agreed to jointly coordinate 
measures, including stepping up vigil along the contiguous border districts of India and 
Nepal, to prevent misuse of the open India-Nepal border for activities directed against 
India. On their part, the Government of Ne pal have assured that their territory would 
not be used for activities inimical to India's interest and have been extending their

discussion with Bhutan. Both sides share concern on this issue. India and

Joint Press Statement 
 His Excellency Mr. Girija Prasad Koirala, Prime Minister of Nepal, is paying 
an official goodwill visit to India from 31 July to 6 August, 2000 at the invitation of His

 During his visit, the Prime Minister of Nepal visited Rajghat and paid homage 
to the memory of Mahatma Gandhi. The Prime Minister of Nepal called on the President 
and the Vice President of India. He had a meeting with the Prime Minister of India, which 
was followed by delegation-level talks, led by the two Prime Ministers, on bilaterial and 
other issues of mutual interest. Ministers of Home Affairs, External Affairs, Defence, 
Finance, Human Resource Development and Water Resources of the Government of India

Andhra Pradesh visit the Hi-tech City, interact with leaders of business and industry and 
attend a luncheon meeting hosted in his honour by the Federation of the Indian 
Chambers of Commerce and Industries.

warmth and cordiality. During these discussions, the Prime Ministers of India and 
Nepal noted that the age-old and traditional friendship between the peoples of the two 
countries, based on the enduring bonds of history, geography and shared social and 
cultural values, had been reinforced in r ecent times and bilateral cooperation expanded 
to embrace new areas of economic and developmental activities. The Prime Ministers 
reiterated the commitment of their Governme nts to further strengthen the close and 
friendly relations between the two countries, in a spirit of equality, mutual respect and

partnership and on the basis of an enhanced level of trust and understanding, keeping

partnership, which derived sustenance from traditional links and shared values.

FIRST NATIONAL CONFERENCE OF IT MINISTERS 
Common Action Plan to promote IT in India 
The first-ever National Conference of IT Ministers was held in New Delhi today, 
July 15, 2000. The Prime Minister, Shri Atal Bihari Vajpayeee, inaugurated the 
Conference, in which as many as fourteen Ministers of various States also participated. 
333 

RAJYA SABHA [25 August, 2000] 
The Conference thanked the Prime Minister for announcing the following three 
landmark decisions. 
 Full deregulation of National Long Distance Operations (NLDO), before 
August 15, 2000, with no restriction on the number of licenses to be issued. 
 Complete demonopolization of undersea optical fiber connectivity for ISPs 
by August 15, 2000. The private ISPs will be allowed, either singly or jointly, to set up 
their own landing stations anywhere in India in collaboration with international 
undersea bandwidth carriers. 
(3) A Task Force on human resource development in IT to prepare long- 
term strategy for significantly increasing the number of well-trained IT 
professionals. The Task Force will draw a plan to optimally use the existing 
infrastructure of the UTs, RECs, other engineering colleges and educational 
institutions to double their student intake from the next academic year and 
triple it in the next two years. The Task Force will comprise Ministers of HRD, 
IT and Finance, along with representatives from State Governments. 
These decision will go a long way to strengthen the country's telecom 
infrastructure and infrastructure for IT education. 
After comprehensive and highly productive deliberations, the conference 
adopted the following consensus Action Plan to promote IT in India. 
 The Union Government and the State Governments will allow free Right of 
Way facility, with no charge in cash or kind, to access providers to lay optical fiber 
networks along National highways, State highways, and other roads. Only a nominal 
restoration fee will be charged for providing this facility. 
 The physical and civic infrastructure of the existing and emerging IT 
development centres will be improved. 
(3) Development of Indian languages on computers and creation of 
useful content on the Internet in all Indian languages will be promoted. 
(4) Facilities for IT education and IT-based education will be expanded 
and improved. For this, the resources and expertise of the private sector 
educational organizations, will be synergized with those of government and 
other established educational institutions. 
(5) The Union and State Governments will take specific measures to 
promote e-governance to improve transparency, accountability and efficiency.

employments are not less than the floor level wages.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF PERSONNEL AND 
TRAINING AND DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND PENSIONERS' WELFARE OF 
THE MINISTRY OF PERSONNEL, PUBLIC GRIEVANCES AND PENSIONS 
(SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE): (a) to (c) Some of the Central Vigilance 
Commission to eliminate corruption prevailing in public life, alongwith the status 
thereof are as under:— 
(i) Enactment of Central Vigilance Commission Act 
The Central Vigilance Commission Bill, 1999 has been introduced in the Lok 
Sabha on 20th December, 1999. Presently , the Bill stands referred to the Joint 
Committee of both the Houses of Parliament for its consideration and recommendations. 
(ii) Enactment of Freedom of Information Act 
The "Freedom of Information Bill, 2000" has been introduced in Lok Sabha on 
25th July, 2000. 
(iii) Enactment of Whistle Blowers' Act 
On the basis of the practice in Britain and other countries like the United States of 
America, the Central Vigilance Commission has addressed the Law Commission in 
this regard indicating the need for a Whistle Blowers Act to encourage honest public 
servants to expose corrupt practices. 
(iv) Enactment of Corrupt Public Servants (Forfeiture of Property) Act 
After examination of the 166th Report of Law Commission containing 
proposed legislation in this regard, the Department of Personnel and Training felt that 
provision for forfeiture of property illegally acquired by the public servants can be 
created within the frame work of Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 by carrying out 
suitable amendments. The Ministry of Law has agreed with the views of the 
Department of Personnel & Training. However, the matter is further under examination 
in consultation with legal experts. 
(v) Implementation of Benami Transaction (Prohibition) Act, (1988) 
The Benami Transaction (Prohibition) Act, 1988 was passed by the Parliament 
in the year 1988. The Act provides for prohibition of benami transactions and the right 
to recover property held provides benami. In terms of 
359 

RAJYA SABHA [25 August, 2000] 
Section 8 of the Act, the Central Government is required to make rules for carrying out 
the purposes thereof. 
The Department of Revenue has informed that rules could not be framed owing to 
legal shortcomings that were indicated by the Ministry of Law. However, modifications 
to the Act have been suggested by the Department of Revenue to take care of 
shortcomings in the Act and the proposal is stated to have been sent by that Department 
to the Ministry of Law for vetting.

[25 August, 2000] R AJYA SABHA 
MINISTER OF STATE OF THE DEPARTMENT OF DISINVESTMENT (SHRI ARUN 
SHOURIE): (a) The Planning System in India and the planning process as practiced, has 
been one of the pillars of our approach to economic de velopment and growth since 
independence and has stood us in good stead. We can take justifiable pride in having 
successfully reversed the worst inequities of our colonial heritage and building a nation of 
considerable economic strength in a framework of democracy and federalism. We 
cannot, however, overlook our shortcomings or to the magnitude of the challenges that 
lie ahead of us. 
The planning process culminates in the formulation of Five Year Plans which in 
turn are operationalised through its Annual Plans. So far we have implemented eight 
Five Year Plans and are in the middle of our Ninth Five Year Plan. The growth in GDP 
realised in each of the last eight Five Year Plans, except for the Third Plan (1961-1966) 
and the Fourth Plan (1969-1974), was almost as projected or above the projection in 
the respective Plan. 
 The process of Plan formulation involves a well defined consultative 
mechanism that uses inputs/ suggestions from structured consultations with diverse 
interest groups had professionals from various fields including, education, agriculture, 
industry, services, academics and voluntary organisations. This is facilitated through 
the setting up of Working Groups/ Steering Committees on specific issues and sectors. In 
addition, technical inputs at sectoral and macro level emanating from plan models and 
other analysis carried out in the Planning Commission and used to formulate the Five 
Year Plans. Finally, the Plan is consid ered/approved by the National Development 
Council before it is operationalised. 
 The exercise for the preparation of the Tenth Five Plan has just been initiated 
and the consultative process-as indicated above, is to be further deepened and 
broadened with a view to reflect and address effectively the changing context and the 
emerging challenges of our economy.

27-7-2000, has, among other things, urged that the present reservation policy should

reservation/dereservation of items for exclusive manufacture in the SSI sector is 
examined on continual basis by the Government and decisions in this respect are taken 
after considering all relevant aspects.

sector become globally competitive. These include special focus on areas such as 
technology upgradation, infrastructural as sistance through cluster approach, timely

3409. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of PRIME 
MINISTER be pleased to state: 
 whether it is a fact that in an agreement signed with an American 
Company, "Space Imaging", the Department of Space, India has permitted the former 
to take satellite photographs and to manage their sale and distribution; 
 if so, the details thereof and the reasons therefor; 
 whether it is also a fact that the Defence and army authority in India had 
expressed grave reservation about this measure, which in their opinion, would 
compromise national security; and 
 if so, under what comp elling circumstances was the objection from the 
defence authorities overruled? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF SPACE 
(SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE): (a) and (b) No, Sir. However, an agreement is under 
finalisation between Antrix Corporation of Department of Space with "Space 
Imaging", a US Company for regulating the dissemination of 1 Mtr. Spatial resolution 
data from IKONOS satellite. 
395 

RAJYA SABHA [25 August, 2000] 
(c) and (d) Under the United Nations (UN) principles relating to remote sensing 
of the Earth from Outer Space, there is no restriction on any satellite imaging over any 
country and therefore, the question of permission for any satellite to take pictures from 
Outer Space does not arise. However, there is a need for regulating the distribution of 
the High-resolution data to the users in the country in order to take care of the national 
security. Hence, Government of India have examined the matter and decided on the 
Policy for acquisition and dissemination of satellite remote sensing images, including 
high-resolution images to support developmental activities. The Policy was formulated 
after detailed discussions with all the concerned Ministries/Departments. As per the 
Policy the high-resolution data (including the data from IKONOS of Space Imaging) 
will be distributed through Antrix Corporation/National Remote Sensing Agency, 
Department of Space, after taking into account national security considerations.

RULING BY CHAIRMAN 
On Matter of Privilege involving issues related to 
National Telecom Policy, 1999 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon'ble Members may recall that on 18.8.2000, a matter 
of Privilege involving issues related to th e National Telecom Policy, 1999, was raised 
by Shri Nilotpal Basu. Shri Basu, quoting a news report, stated that the Government 
had announced the guidelines for National Long Distance Service outside the House, 
when it was in session and that, in these guidelines, the Government had departed 
from the approved National Telecom Policy, 1999, in particular, in   para 3.5.   Shri 
Suresh Pachouri also 
426 

[25 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
lent support to the contention of Shri Basu in this behalf. The Minister for 
Communications stated that there was no departure from the policy and that the 
guidelines prescribed a procedure. The Minister stated that he had also received a 
Calling Attention Notice in response to which he had forwarded a copy of the 
guidelines. I had reserved my ruling on the issue raised by Shri Basu. Subsequently, a 
notice under Rule 187 for breach of privilege of the House has been received from 
Shri Basu on the subject on 21.8.2000. 
I have seen the news item cited by Shri Basu in the House and also referred 
to in his notice. I have also seen para 3.5 of the New Telecom Policy 1999 and the 
copy of the guidelines sent by the Minister in his reply to the Calling Attention Notice. 
The wording in the news item in question varies from the provisions actually given in 
the guidelines. The guidelines appear to be in the nature of an operational, rather than 
a policy, document. Also para 3.5 of the New Telecom Policy does not explicitly say 
that intra-circle STD will be only reserved for fixed service providers. As such, the 
provisions in the guidelines do not appear to be a violation or alteration of the New 
Telecom Policy 1999. 
Hon. Members, it has been held by the presiding officers of both the Houses 
on a number of occasions, including on 10.8.70, 19.8.70 and 19.8.85, in this House 
that no privilege of the House is involved if statements on matters of public interest 
are not made first in the House. Normally it is the practice that when Parliament is in 
session, the Government should make all policy statements in the House and not doing 
so would be highly improper. However, in the present case, the statement made by the 
Minister to the Press, though a matter of publ ic interest, is not a policy statement, and 
it would seem that the impression in this regard is based on a newspaper report, which 
does not exactly reproduce faithfully the text of the guidelines. Therefore, I find that 
the announcement of the guidelines for a National Long Distance Service by the 
Government outside the House does not appear to constitute a breach of privilege of 
the House, and the matter may be treated as closed.

SHRIMATI MANEKA GANDHI: Madam, the Rehabilitation Council of India 
Act, 1992 came into force with effect from the 31 st July, 1993. The main functions of 
the RCI include standardization of training courses at different levels. Regularization 
of standards of training in all the training institutions throughout the country, 
recognition of institutions/universities for th eir training courses within and outside the 
country on a reciprocal basis and maintenance of a Central Rehabilitation Register for 
professionals possessing recognized qualification in the area of rehabilitation. 
The experience gained by way of implementation of the RCI Act has brought out 
the need for making certain amendments in the Act, with a view to making its 
implementation more effective and broad-based and to bring it in consonance with the 
Persons with Disabilities Act. In so far as the definitions are concerned, with a view to 
avoiding legal complications, as a part of our consultation process with experts and 
NGOs working in the disability rehabilitation, we have set up an expert committee to 
advise us. I would like to express my appreciation for the suggestions given by the 
committee, many of whose major suggestions for amendments have been accepted and 
incorporated in the Amendment Bill. We have proposed to strengthen the activities of 
the RCI by adding research and rehabilita tion and promotion of  special education 
within its ambit. I am happy to inform you that the RCI has undertaken a major 
programme for training of the PHC do ctors and other personnel working in 
rehabilitation throughout the country. In the present Act, the Central Ministries 
representatives are three—the Ministry of Fi nance, the Ministry of Health and Family 
Welfare and the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment. There are a number of 
Central Ministries which are vitally concerned with different facets of problems being 
faced by persons with disabilities as rehabili tation is a multi-sectoral task. The expert 
committee recommended raising the number to five. In the proposed amendment, 
seven Ministries are represented. The names of these Ministries/Departments have not 
been specified in the Amendment Bill so that in case any change in the representation 
is considered necessary, the Act need hot be amended time and again. In addition to 
the original three Ministries, the other Mi nistries will be given representation by 
rotation and this will be specified in the revised Rules which will be framed after the 
amendment. There is no intention to bureaucratize the control over the Council but to 
ensure association of other concerned Central Ministries/Departments for more 
effective coordination within the schemes meant for the welfare of the persons with 
disabilities.

The RCI Act is a regulatory Act. Any dilution in the training standards may 
adversely affect the quality of rehabilitation services to  persons with disabilities. 
Therefore, the penal provision has been retained with a view to have some teeth to 
ensure its effective implementation. 
My Ministry is implementing, various programmes for the welfare of the persons 
with disabilities. We have a continuous dial ogue with the NGOs in this regard. This 
process will continue. The Government has an open mind to review the 
implementation of the Act as and when required. Any useful suggestion from the 
hon'ble Members is welcome.

DR. A.R. KIDWAI (Delhi): Mr. Vice- Chairman, Sir, thank you for giving 
me this opportunity to speak on this Bill. I would like to congratulate the hon. Minister

appreciate, all of us must ap preciate, the efforts which the hon. Minister is making for 
their rehabilitation. In India, because of un hygienic conditions and because of poverty, 
the number of people who are physically handicapped is much larger than anywhere 
else. The people who are physically handicapped can be utilised to do productive work 
so that they can live a honourable life in the society provided they are given some 
training to do certain activities. It has been found that those who are physically 
handicapped, if they lose on e ability, they develop other abil ities much better and they 
can do better. Take the case of those persons who are blind. Their sensory nerve 
improves. Their memory improves and they can remember things much better than 
many others. Those who cannot move physically, can do many things. They can do 
more productive work sitting at home. Those who cannot speak, are ideal persons to be 
utilised at places like printing press, etc. because they can be very good typists. They 
can edit the material for printing without disclosing the secrets and examination papers 
to anybody else. Such peopl e are being utilised in other parts of the world more 
effectively. So we should take advantage of the capabilities of these persons. I am 
happy that in India there are several institutions which are doing good work. Unless 
they are given proper attention and help by the' Government, they cannot succeed. Our 
objective shoutd be to give training to phys ically handicapped people and rehabilitate 
them in productive work so that they can go back to their families and be productive

bureaucratic negligence they are languishing.   Therefore, I would like to take

VALEDICTORY REMARKS 
THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN : The session commenced on 24 lh July, 2000 and 
we have had 22 sittings spread over more than 102 hours. During the session, 22 
reports of various Parliamentary Committees were presented or laid on the Table of the 
House. If I am not mistaken, we sat for 22 days in this session. During the session, we 
have transacted a lot of Legislative Business and passed about 22 Government Bills, 
including two Constitution (Amendment) Bi lls and three Bills creating three new 
States, that is, Chhattisgarh, Uttaranchal an d Jharkhand and returned four Bills. There 
were seven statements in all, of the Prime Minister and other Ministers, which 
occasioned a number of clarifications being sought by Members. We had four Calling 
Attentions on the death of precious wild life in various parts of the country, including 
Zoos and wildlife sanctuaries, the recent incidents of bomb blasts in various parts of 
the country and action taken by the Government, the situation arising out of the closure 
of several units of Khadi and Village industries in the country; and further relaxation 
in Jute package order and its adverse effects on jute farmers, workers and the industry 
in general. 
We had two Short Duration Discussions on the Disinvestment Policy of the 
Government; and the fall in the prices of agricultural prod uce resulting in huge 
monetary losses affecting the earnings of the farmers, but the discussion remained 
inconclusive. 
There were also more than 78, maybe a little more Special Mentions on matters 
of public importance. 
Three references were made in the Hous e on the first anniversary of India's 
victory in Kargil, homage to martyrs of freedom movement and victims of atomic 
bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki and on killing of innocent people in J and 
K by the militants and forces inimical to India. 
During the session, we have also adopted one Statutory Resolution, namely, to 
amend the First Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act, 1975. 
During the session, three newly-elected Members from the State of Kerala took   
oath/affirmation and took their seats in the House. 
During the session, 460 Starred Questions, 3565 Unstarred Questions

Madam Chairperson, as this Session comes to an end, we can look back with a 
reasonable sense of satisfaction that two important Constitution Amendment Bills 
were passed and that this House and the other House made history when three Bills, 
creating three new States, were also passed with the cooperation of all the sections of

be that of a responsible and constructive Opposition. To the best of our ability, we 
have tried to play that role as well as we can. I thank the hon. Leader of the House for

Parliamentary Affairs. I think their joint efforts contributed a great deal to the smooth 
functioning of this House. Madam, we thank the hon. Chairman, you and the 
Secretary-General and his staff. We owe a special debt of gratitude for all the guidance 
that we have received from the Chairman and your goodself, Madam. 
Of course, we have some disappointments. But I do understand the reasons being 
beyond our control. The fact that the Women's Reservation Bill is still not on the anvil 
is a matter of disappointment to us. But I draw  satisfaction from the fact that when this 
matter was raised in the House, the hon. Prime Minister gave a categorical assurance 
that the Government would try to evolve a consensus, but if that consensus could not 
be evolved, the Government would nevertheless come forward with the Bill for 
consideration of Parliament. Madam, we were keen that before the Prime Minister 
went on his foreign tour, there ought to have been an exhaustive discussion on foreign 
policy. It is a matter of disappointment that though this discussion was also scheduled, 
for no fault of the Government, it could not take place. 
There are also other important discussions which we wanted. For example, on the 
National Agriculture Policy, our farmers are facing considerable difficulties. The 
National Agriculture Policy sets out a visi on. But we need a concrete programme of 
action to give shape to that vision. And it would have been a great advantage if the 
House had an opportunity to discuss the National Agriculture Policy. We are also very 
keen—we are now in the third year of the Ninth Five Year Plan-that the Ninth Five 
Year Plan, after a long delay, should come up for discussion in this House. This has 
not been possible. But I am not blaming the Government. I do understand that there are 
reasons why some of these things could not be taken up.
